threads_text: Security researchers found a booby-trapped AGENTS.md file in someone's Downloads folder that told their coding agent to install malware. In tests it worked on Codex about 9 times in 10 and got Claude Code to approve a risky change about half the time. Do you ever run Claude Code or Codex from your Downloads folder?
caption:
Security firm Forever Security caught a coding agent trying to install a malicious npm package on a customer's computer.
The order came from a planted AGENTS.md file sitting in the Downloads folder, where the agent was running.
In tests, the trick worked on OpenAI's Codex in more than 90% of attempts and on Claude Code about half the time.

slides.headline: One hidden file in your Downloads folder can turn *Claude Code and Codex* against you

slides.heading: Caught on a *real computer*
paras: Forever Security stopped a coding agent from installing a malicious npm package called function-color on a customer's machine.
The order came from an AGENTS.md file in the Downloads folder, where the agent had been started.

slides.heading: Why *Downloads* is the weak spot
paras: Coding agents automatically read and follow the instruction file in the folder they open.
And a web page can save a file into Downloads by itself. The researchers built a test page that did exactly that.
slides.note: How the real file got there is still unknown.

slides.heading: Codex fell for it *90% of the time*
paras: In tests, Codex followed the planted file in more than 90% of attempts.
A fake CLAUDE.md got Claude Code to approve a settings change about half the time, exposing its login token to the researchers' server.

slides.heading: Nothing to *patch*
paras: Forever says there is nothing for OpenAI or Anthropic to fix, because the agents worked as designed.

paras.t: Its advice: never start an agent in Downloads, and read any AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md you did not write.

paragraphs.text: Security firm Forever Security said it stopped an AI coding agent from installing a malicious npm package on a customer's computer and traced the instruction to a file named AGENTS.md in the customer's Downloads folder. The Downloads folder was also the agent's working directory, according to BleepingComputer, which reported the findings on October 25, 2026. The Hacker News and Cyberpress covered the report on October 26.

The package the agent tried to install was called function-color. According to The Hacker News and Cyberpress, it belongs to a malware campaign that Checkmarx and CloudSEK have tracked under the name MALFEX. The package pulls in a downloader called function-flag, which fetches and launches a Windows payload. Forever said the installation was blocked before any code ran.

Coding agents automatically load instruction files such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md from the folder they start in and treat them as guidance for the project. The Hacker News reported that the planted file was disguised as ordinary engineering notes, with one section telling the agent to add a server to its own configuration and install the package.

The second piece is the browser. Chrome, Edge and Firefox save downloads to the Downloads folder by default without asking, though they show a notification, BleepingComputer reported. It found that Brave asked for approval first. Forever built a proof of concept page that saved an AGENTS.md file to Downloads on its own. The researchers said they could not determine how the file reached the original customer's machine, and the website route was shown only in testing.
How Codex and Claude Code responded

Against OpenAI's Codex, the file told the agent to register a server in its global configuration file, which applies to every Codex session on the machine. Forever reported success in more than 90% of its Codex tests. Cyberpress said most of those tests used a harmless payload that opened the calculator app, while the real malicious package was tested separately inside an isolated virtual machine.

Against Anthropic's Claude Code, a crafted CLAUDE.md framed as internal gateway setup tried to get the agent to write a new API address into a project settings file. That redirected traffic to a server the researchers controlled, exposing the session's login token, which Cyberpress said they replayed successfully. The Hacker News noted that Claude Code usually asks a human to approve such changes and often refuses suspicious ones, but the long engineering document framing got the change approved about half the time.

Running agents from Downloads is not rare, according to the researchers. BleepingComputer reported that Forever's data shows hundreds of its customers starting agents there, and that Claude Code alone launched more than 1,300 sessions from that folder.

Forever said there is nothing for OpenAI or Anthropic to patch, since the agents followed their instruction files as designed. Its recommendations include never starting an agent in Downloads, running agents from a specific project folder, reading any AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md file the user did not write, keeping approval prompts and sandboxes switched on, and rotating login tokens if a planted file is found.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the case shows that the instruction files that make coding agents useful also give anyone who can write a file into the right folder a way to speak to the agent. Because the weakness sits in how people use these tools rather than in a single bug, the fix depends on habits and default settings.
Watch whether OpenAI and Anthropic change their agents to warn users or refuse to load instruction files when a session starts in a Downloads or home folder.
